action: Keep firm-soled closed slippers by the bed and every door
why: Walking barefoot, in socks or thin slippers can cause cuts they won't feel.

source.title: IWGDF 2023 Guideline on the prevention of foot ulcers in persons with diabetes
source.quote: not walking barefoot, not walking in socks without shoes, and not walking in thin-soled slippers, either at home or outside

reassign_reason: One-sided weakness or poor eyesight makes a reliable self-check hard
action: Check both feet daily, including soles and between toes
why: Numb feet hide small wounds until they become serious.

source.title: IWGDF 2023 Prevention Guideline; Diabetes UK — How to look after your feet
source.section: IWGDF Recommendation 6 (daily foot inspection); Diabetes UK step 3
source.quote: check them every day… or get someone else to check your feet for you

reassign_reason: One-sided weakness makes reaching and drying both feet unsafe
action: Wash feet daily and dry carefully between the toes
why: Moisture between toes lets skin break down.

source.title: IWGDF 2023 Guideline on the prevention of foot ulcers in persons with diabetes
source.quote: wash their feet daily (with careful drying, particularly between the toes)

reassign_reason: Poor eyesight or a weak grip makes nail cutting risky
action: Cut toenails straight across
why: Reduces ingrown nails and cuts.

source.title: IWGDF 2023 Guideline on the prevention of foot ulcers in persons with diabetes
source.quote: cut toenails straight across

action: Choose seamless socks; avoid tight socks
why: Seams and tight bands press on skin they can't feel.

source.title: IWGDF 2023 Guideline on the prevention of foot ulcers in persons with diabetes
source.quote: wear socks that are seamless and not too tight

action: Keep a long-handled mirror in the bedroom for checking soles
why: Lets them see the soles without bending far.

source.title: Diabetes UK — How to look after your feet
source.section: Step 3: Check your feet every day
source.quote: If you struggle to lift your feet up, try using a mirror to check the bottom of your feet

action: Feel inside shoes before putting them on
why: A stone or pin inside won't be felt.

source.title: IWGDF 2023 Guideline on the prevention of foot ulcers in persons with diabetes
source.quote: check the inside of the shoe for any foreign objects each time before they don the footwear

action: Add night-lights on the route from bed to toilet
why: Poor eyesight plus darkness raises fall risk.

source.title: Thomas Pocklington Trust — Lighting in and around the home: a guide for people with sight loss; RNIB — Safety at home
source.quote: improving lighting in areas such as the bathroom and at the top and bottom of stairs

action: Brighten lighting on stairs and mark step edges with contrasting tape
why: Step edges are hard to see with reduced vision.

source.title: Thomas Pocklington Trust — Lighting in and around the home; RNIB — Safety at home
source.quote: Appropriate domestic lighting, especially near the top and bottom of stairs, is very important to falls avoidance

action: Fit grab rails beside the toilet and in the shower
why: Falls after stroke are common; rails give a fixed hold when sitting down or standing up.

source.title: NHS — Falls: prevention; Stroke Association — Equipment for stroke survivors at home
source.quote: consider fitting grab rails in the bathroom

action: Use a shower seat; no standing showers
why: One-sided weakness makes balance unreliable on wet floors.

source.title: Stroke Association — Equipment for stroke survivors at home
source.quote: Bath and shower seats so you can sit down while bathing

action: Remove the bathroom door lock or fit one that opens from outside
why: If they fall inside, you need to get in.

source.title: Scottish Government — Enhancing the accessibility, adaptability and usability of Scotland's homes (housing design guidance)
source.quote: Locks on bathroom doors should be capable of being released from the outside in case of emergency.

action: Fit a bath seat or bath board and a grab rail at the bath; nobody steps over the side without a hand to hold
why: Stepping over a bath edge on one leg is where balance fails after stroke; sitting to get in and out removes that moment.

source.title: Stroke Association — Equipment for stroke survivors at home
source.quote: Grab rails to help you get in and out of the shower or bath … Bath and shower seats so you can sit down while bathing

action: Ask the stroke team for a transfer-equipment assessment (hoist, chair raiser, transfer aids) and training for whoever helps them move
why: Bed-to-chair and chair-to-toilet moves are when both of you can fall; the right equipment and a taught technique protect you both.

source.title: NICE NG236 — Stroke rehabilitation in adults
source.quote: Assess people after stroke for their equipment needs and to see whether their family or carers need training to use the equipment … Equipment may include hoists, chair raisers and small aids

action: Put a written daily checklist where they sit and set phone alarms for the routine items
why: After stroke, memory and attention work better with prompts in the room than with reminders from people.

source.title: NICE NG236 — Stroke rehabilitation in adults
source.quote: external aids (for example, diaries, lists, calendars and alarms) … environmental strategies (using routines and environmental prompts)

action: Meals and drinks only sitting upright at the table with the TV off — never lying down or when drowsy
why: Food or drink going the wrong way can cause pneumonia; posture and attention are the parts of swallowing safety the household controls.

source.title: Stroke Association — Swallowing problems
source.section: Learn how to swallow safely (dos and don'ts)
source.quote: Turn off the TV … Sit up with a straight back … Don't try to eat or drink if you're feeling tired or drowsy. Try to eat or drink lying down.

action: Remove loose rugs and cables from walking routes
why: Trips are a leading cause of falls after stroke.

source.title: NHS — Falls: prevention
source.quote: do not have too much clutter at home, or things you could trip on such as loose wires or rugs

action: Provide a firm, higher chair with armrests
why: Soft, low seats are hard to get out of with weak limbs.

source.title: Worcestershire Acute Hospitals NHS Trust — Occupational therapy: Choosing a chair
source.quote: the seat should be firm and flat; armrests make it easier to push into standing

action: Put phone, lamp and water within reach on the stronger side
why: They can reach help without twisting or getting up.

source.title: American Stroke Association — Modify the bedroom to match your abilities
source.quote: Keep a cell phone or corded phone within reach at bedside

action: Switch to elastic waists and velcro or popper closures
why: Buttons and zips are hard with a weak hand.

source.title: Stroke Association — Guide to dressing after stroke
source.quote: Avoid buttons and zips… substitute these for touch-close alternatives like Velcro or poppers

action: Learn the common problems after stroke: frequent falls, shoulder pain, stiffness, incontinence
why: Spotting them early means getting help sooner.

source.title: NICE NG236 — Stroke rehabilitation in adults (2023)
source.quote: Provide information so that people after stroke, and their family and carers, can recognise the complications of the condition, including frequent falls, spasticity, shoulder pain and incontinence

action: Caregiver does the daily foot check, soles and between toes
why: One-sided weakness makes bending with a mirror unsafe, and a foot they cannot see is a foot nobody checks.

source.title: IWGDF 2023 Practical Guidelines on the prevention and management of diabetes-related foot disease
source.quote: Determine if the person is able to perform a foot inspection. If not, discuss who can assist the person in this task. Persons who have substantial visual impairment or physical inability to visualise their feet cannot adequately do the inspection

action: Clear the hallway of rugs and clutter this week
why: A trip is now dangerous twice: a fall, and an injury they may not feel.

source.title: NHS — Falls: prevention; IWGDF 2023 Practical Guidelines (minor trauma in neuropathy)
source.section: NHS: preventing falls at home; IWGDF §1 pathophysiology: "in people with neuropathy, minor trauma (e.g., from ill-fitting shoes, or an acute mechanical or thermal injury) can precipitate ulceration of the foot". source.quote: do not have too much clutter at home, or things you could trip on such as loose wires or rugs
